scenarios.name: Before any deal the deck holds all 16 cards
After 18 rounds (two hands of 9 rounds) the match is in hand 3
Seat 1 is forehand in hand 2, so it declares when both pass
After the deal each seat holds 4 hand cards and the deck is empty
Each seat's private hand holds exactly 4 cards after the deal
Both seats are offered every bid and the bids are recorded
Higher bidder (seat 1, 79 over 53) is declarer at 79
Equal bids of 66: forehand seat 2 declares at 66
Both pass: forehand seat 2 declares at 53
Both bids are announced along with the declarer
Declarer seat 2 picks Wenz; the defender is not asked for a contract
A Hearts Solo hand plays all 8 tricks for any deal: every hand card is used and hand 2 begins
A Wenz hand plays all 8 tricks for any deal
Defender seat 1 gives Stoss: multiplier 2; the declarer is not asked
Defender seat 1 gives No Stoss: multiplier 1
Hand cards and stack cards together supply all 8 tricks: no hand card is left after the hand
Lead passes correctly through the 8 tricks for any deal, and the hand completes
A Bells Solo hand with trumps as one suit completes all tricks for any deal
Following under the follow-suit rule always leaves a legal card: the hand completes
Trick winners are decided in a Leaves Solo for any deal and the hand completes
Trick points accrue over a full hand for any deal (hand completes)
Face-down cards turn up so all 8 tricks can be played
Without Stoss at bid 53 a seat gains at most 3 per hand, so a 13-point lead holds for any deal

After 36 rounds more match points wins: a 100-point head start cannot be caught

spec_choices.why: The designer set 2. The deal uses all 16 cards for exactly two players, so neither more nor fewer seats fit.

A thoughtful player judges their hand plus the open stack cards before bidding high, picks the contract that fits their trumps, gives Stoß only when the declarer looks overstretched, and times the playing of stack cards to unlock the hidden cards beneath.
Talk is not part of the rules, and with two opponents it only adds words.
This makes 'higher bid' a numeric comparison.

spec_choices.what: Trump ranks encoded as trump_strength 20 down to 11, and plain ranks as Ace 3, Ten 2, Ober 1
spec_choices.why: This lets the trick winner be decided by arithmetic while keeping exactly the source's order.
Card totals can never reach 1000 (at most 416), so match points come first and card points only break ties. An exact tie is a shared result, which matches the source's draw.

spec_choices.what: Trick card points and trick counts are public
spec_choices.why: Both players see every played card, so these totals are open information.

simplifications.what: The bidding steps and the trick steps share one flat round list, each step gated by a 'when' condition on round_in_hand
simplifications.why: The engine runs one round script. Per-step arithmetic conditions keep 36 rounds exactly as the source counts them.

simplifications.what: Hand scoring runs as an update at the end of trick round 8
simplifications.why: This keeps the round count at 36 without adding a separate scoring round.

simplifications.what: Face-down stack cards are held as hidden table attributes rather than player attributes
simplifications.why: Not even their owner may see them, and a player attribute cannot be hidden from its owner.

variation.original_summary: Officers' Schafkopf is a two-player version of the Bavarian trick-taking game. Each player has a private hand plus rows of face-down cards topped by face-up cards. The non-dealer announces a contract (a Suit Solo or a Wenz) and may be doubled (Stoß), then 16 tricks are played with must-follow rules. The declarer needs 61 of the 120 card points to win.

review.evidence: Contract choice, the Stoß and card play all change the outcome, and no trivial policy wins. But the non-dealer is forced to declare on whatever cards they get, and the dealer always gets to react. In a single deal the seat and the cards decide much of the result, and a lone hand has no way to even out who declares.

Card play rewards counting and inference over a long game. But one deal of 32 cards decides the winner, and a declarer handed a weak hand with no way out usually loses whatever their skill. Luck of the deal dominates a one-hand match.

Trump management, counting card points, reading the opponent's hand from the visible up cards and from their contract, and timing which up cards to release give a deep skill ceiling. A beginner can still take tricks and points.
Hand cards are private and the down cards are unknown even to their owner. Players must infer holdings from the contract, the Stoß decision and the play, and plan which down cards they will uncover.
The card-point total against the 61 threshold is pure arithmetic.

32 tracked cards, two rows of four stacks per player and 16 tricks make a state far larger than the attribute limit. The optional 'deal as hands' rule is ambiguous, and with only one deal there is no match structure.

problems: The state is too large: 32 cards in four stack positions per player plus a hand exceeds the platform's attribute and step limits.
One deal decides everything, so luck of the cards swamps skill.
The non-dealer is forced to declare whatever they hold, so a bad deal for the forced declarer is close to an automatic loss. This is a seat and deal edge with no decision to correct it.
Winning is binary (61 or not). It gives no reward for judging how strong a hand is, so there is little to reason about before play beyond picking the trump suit.
The rules are underspecified for building: 'or deal as hands' is optional, the trump order is not stated, and the scoring of doubles is not stated.

changes.what: Shrink the deck to 16 cards (Ace, Ten, Ober, Unter in four suits, 104 card points). Each player gets 4 private hand cards and 2 stacks of one face-down card under one face-up card. A hand is 8 tricks and the declarer needs 53.
changes.why: Keeps the private hand, the face-up and face-down stacks, the revealing of the down card and the Solo/Wenz trump structures, while bringing the state and step count within the limits.
changes.fixes: The state is too large: 32 cards in four stack positions per player plus a hand exceeds the platform's attribute and step limits.

changes.what: Play a match of 4 hands with the dealer alternating, scored in match points.
changes.why: Several deals average out card luck, and each player is forehand twice, so no seat has an edge over the match.
changes.fixes: One deal decides everything, so luck of the cards swamps skill.

changes.what: Add a simultaneous sealed bid before the contract: Pass, 53, 66 or 79 card points. The higher bid declares, ties go to forehand, and if both pass, forehand must declare at 53. A higher bid is worth more match points if made and costs as much if failed.
changes.why: A weak hand can now hand the declaration to the opponent. Bidding forces each player to judge their own strength from partial information and to guess the opponent's bid. Hand evaluation becomes a scored skill.
changes.fixes: The non-dealer is forced to declare whatever they hold, so a bad deal for the forced declarer is close to an automatic loss. This is a seat and deal edge with no decision to correct it.

changes.what: Use graded match points: a bid of 53 is worth 2, 66 is worth 3 and 79 is worth 4, plus 1 for taking all 8 tricks, all doubled by Stoß. The winner is the player with more match points, then more total card points.
changes.why: This rewards accurate judgement of how much the hand can make rather than a single win/lose line. The Stoß becomes a risk decision with a real price either way.
changes.fixes: Winning is binary (61 or not). It gives no reward for judging how strong a hand is, so there is little to reason about before play beyond picking the trump suit.

changes.what: State every rule explicitly: the dealing layout, the trump orders for Solo and Wenz, the following rules, and when a down card is revealed and becomes playable.
changes.why: So the game can be built and played without guessing.
changes.fixes: The rules are underspecified for building: 'or deal as hands' is optional, the trump order is not stated, and the scoring of doubles is not stated.

keeps: Two-player Schafkopf trick play with must-follow-suit rules and the winner of a trick leading next.
The Officers' layout: face-down cards under face-up cards, a down card turned up when the card above it is played and playable from the next trick.
The contract choice between a Suit Solo (Obers, Unters and the trump suit are trumps) and a Wenz (only Unters are trumps).
The Stoß doubling by the defender.
Card-point counting with Ace 11, Ten 10, Ober 3 and Unter 2, and a declarer needing just over half the points.

recommendation.reason: The core (hidden hands, unknown down cards, contract and double, trick play) is rich in inference. A reduced 16-card deck over a 4-hand match fits the limits and keeps the game recognisable.

variation.name: Officers' Schafkopf: Bidding Match
variation.summary: A two-player Schafkopf match of 4 short hands with a 16-card deck and the Officers' face-down/face-up layout. Players bid simultaneously for the right to declare, the declarer picks a Solo or Wenz, the defender may Stoß, and 8 tricks are played. Match points decide the winner.
variation.rules:
DECK. There are 16 cards: Ace, Ten, Ober and Unter in each of four suits (Acorns, Leaves, Hearts, Bells). Card points are Ace 11, Ten 10, Ober 3 and Unter 2, which makes 104 in the deck.

MATCH. The match is 4 hands. Each hand is one bidding round followed by 8 trick rounds, which makes 36 rounds in total. Player 1 deals hands 1 and 3 and Player 2 deals hands 2 and 4. The non-dealer is called forehand.

DEAL (start of each hand's bidding round, the only random event of the round). Shuffle the 16 cards. Each player receives:
- 4 private hand cards, seen only by their owner;
- 2 stacks, each made of one face-down card under one face-up card.
The face-up cards (4 in total) are visible to both players. Face-down cards are unknown to both players, including their owner.

BIDDING ROUND.
(1) Both players secretly and simultaneously choose a bid: Pass, 53, 66 or 79. The bid is the number of card points the player promises to take as declarer.
(2) The higher bid becomes declarer at that bid. If the bids are equal and not Pass, forehand is declarer at that bid. If both pass, forehand is declarer at 53. Both bids are then announced.
(3) The declarer chooses a contract and it is announced:
- Acorns Solo, Leaves Solo, Hearts Solo or Bells Solo: trumps are, from highest to lowest, Ober of Acorns, Ober of Leaves, Ober of Hearts, Ober of Bells, Unter of Acorns, Unter of Leaves, Unter of Hearts, Unter of Bells, then the Ace and the Ten of the chosen suit. The three other suits each hold only Ace above Ten.
- Wenz: trumps are, from highest to lowest, Unter of Acorns, Unter of Leaves, Unter of Hearts, Unter of Bells. Each suit holds Ace above Ten above Ober.
(4) The defender chooses Stoß (double) or No Stoß, and the choice is announced. The multiplier is 2 with Stoß and 1 without.

TRICK ROUNDS (8 per hand).
Available cards: a player may play any of their private hand cards or any face-up card on top of one of their stacks.
Lead: in the first trick forehand leads; afterwards the winner of the previous trick leads. The leader plays one available card.
Follow: the other player then plays one available card. All trumps count as one suit, the trump suit, so in a Solo an Ober or Unter is never a card of its printed suit. If the follower has an available card of the led suit, they must play one. Otherwise they may play any available card.
Trick winner: if any trump was played, the higher trump wins. Otherwise the higher card of the led suit wins. The winner adds the card points of both cards to their card-point total for this hand.
Reveal: after the trick, any face-down card whose face-up card was played this trick is turned face up. It is available from the next trick on.

HAND SCORING (after trick 8).
- If the declarer's card points are at least their bid, the declarer scores the contract value in match points. Otherwise the defender scores it.
- Contract value = base, plus 1 if the player who scores took all 8 tricks, multiplied by the Stoß multiplier.
- The base is 2 for a bid of 53, 3 for a bid of 66 and 4 for a bid of 79.
Each player's card points for the hand are also added to their running card-point total for the match. Then all cards are collected for the next deal.
variation.objective: After 4 hands, the player with more match points wins. If match points are equal, the player with the higher total card points over all 4 hands wins. If both are equal, the match is a draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Players must estimate the value of a hand from 4 private cards, 4 visible up cards and 4 unknown down cards, and bid against an opponent's sealed estimate. Overbidding gives away up to 4 match points (8 if doubled), and underbidding or passing lets the opponent declare cheaply. The Stoß becomes a real read on whether the declarer overbid. Card play rewards counting, inferring the opponent's hand from their bid, contract and Stoß decision, and timing when to release up cards to uncover what lies beneath. Simple policies lose:
- Always bidding 79 fails most hands and pays the opponent 4 each time.
- Always passing lets the opponent declare at will, and when forehand it is forced to declare at 53 on any cards.
- Always using Stoß gets punished by strong declarers, and never using it gives up the doubled points from failed contracts.
Alternating the dealer and playing 4 hands removes the seat edge and reduces deal luck. Bidding lets a player with weak cards still gain by defending well and doubling overbids. There is no talk phase because the game has two players with strictly opposed interests.

balanced.evidence:
ARITHMETIC CHECKS. Each suit is 11+10+3+2 = 26 points, and 4 x 26 = 104. Each player gets 4 hand cards and 2 stacks of 2, so 8 cards each, 16 in all, which matches 8 tricks. The 53 threshold is one more than half (52), so 52-52 is a failed contract. That is a real threshold and not a free win.

Solo trumps are 4 Obers, 4 Unters and the trump-suit Ace and Ten: 10 cards worth 12+8+21 = 41 points. The 6 non-trumps (Ace and Ten of three suits) are worth 63. Wenz trumps are the 4 Unters (8 points); the 12 suit cards are worth 96. Rankings are complete and consistent with Schafkopf.

HAND PAYOFF TABLE (declarer's view, match points; the defender scores the same amount on a failure):
- Bid 53: base 2; made +2 / x2 = +4; slam +3 / +6; failed -2 / -4.
- Bid 66: base 3; made +3 / +6; slam +4 / +8; failed -3 / -6.
- Bid 79: base 4; made +4 / +8; slam +5 / +10; failed -4 / -8.
The stakes rise by 1 per level, but the requirement rises by 13 points (about 12.5% of the deck). Climbing the ladder is a genuine risk trade, so no bid dominates.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (more match points, then card points):
(1) Always 79. Hands 79 vs X: this player declares unless tied as dealer. They must hold the opponent to 25 or fewer points, so one Ace plus one Ten in the opponent's tricks (21) and one Ober breaks it. Failure is likely, and a sensible defender then Stoßes, worth about -8 per hand. This loses almost every match against sensible play. Against random play (which bids 79 a quarter of the time and passes otherwise) it still loses most hands.
(2) Always Pass. Against a sensible opponent who bids only strong hands:
- As defender, it scores only when the opponent overreaches.
- As forehand facing a pass, it is forced to declare 53, often with a weak hand, because the sensible dealer passes on purpose.
- It never collects base 3 or 4 on strong hands.
It loses some matches and draws only on equal points. It is not a never-lose policy.
(3) Always Stoß. It doubles losses against declarers who bid on strength, and it wins only against overbidders.
(4) Never Stoß. It forgoes doubling against weak forced-53 declarers, so it loses value.
(5) Always the first contract (Acorns Solo). It discards the contract choice; whoever picks the best of 5 contracts after seeing 8 cards beats it in expectation.
(6) Always lead or follow the first legal card. It loses tricks to card counting.
No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does.

SEAT. Forehand gets tie-breaks on equal bids, the forced 53 when both pass, and the first lead. These are mixed (the forced 53 can hurt), and the role alternates: each player is forehand exactly twice in 4 hands. Information is symmetric: 4 own cards plus 4 public up cards. The tie-break on total card points is fair because every hand distributes exactly 104. Both players can realistically win.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
WHAT THERE IS TO INFER:
- At the bid, each player knows 8 of 16 cards (4 own plus 4 up). The opponent's 4 hidden cards and the 4 face-down cards are unknown.
- The opponent's bid, announced after bidding, signals their strength.
- The contract choice reveals the declarer's trump holding to the defender, who then decides Stoß.
- With only 16 cards, counting is exact. By around trick 4 most of the deck is placed, so card play rewards counting and planning, for example when to uncover a face-down card.

DECISIONS:
- Bid level, a risk choice on a 2/3/4 ladder.
- Contract, the best of 5.
- Stoß, which doubles a swing.
- 8 lead or follow choices per hand.

CHANCE. The deal plus the 4 unknown face-down cards decide hand strength. I estimate deal luck at roughly 40-50% of a single hand, falling over 4 hands because good play mitigates it:
- passing weak hands and defending;
- Stoßing forced or overreaching declarers;
- choosing a Wenz or Solo that fits the cards.

WHEN BOTH PLAY WELL, the deal matters, as in any card game. But outcomes still turn on bid calibration, Stoß decisions and card play. They are not decided by the draw alone.

WHEN SKILL DIFFERS, the policies in the balance check show it matters. A player who overbids, never Stoßes, or plays cards thoughtlessly loses swings of 4-8 match points per hand to one who reasons. A good reasoner is clearly favoured.

design_flags_left: the built game has 5 choice steps per round, over the limit of 4
the built game has 87 attributes, over the limit of 80

triage.reason: The R1 test is correct. In Acorns Solo, Ober of Bells (trump strength 17) beats Unter of Hearts (14), so seat 2 should take the 5 points (49+5=54) and seat 1 stays at 50, below the 53 bid. The game gave the trick to seat 1, and the R12 failures show the same fault: trick resolution ignores the trump strengths.
triage.guidance:
Rework trick resolution.
(1) Classify each played card by the contract. In a Solo, all Obers and Unters plus the Ace and Ten of the chosen suit are trumps. In Wenz, only the four Unters are trumps.
(2) Give each trump its strength from the parameter attributes: Ober Acorns 20 down to Unter Bells 13, then solo-suit Ace 12 and Ten 11.
(3) Winner rules:
- If both cards are trumps, the higher strength wins, whoever led.
- If only one card is a trump, it wins. So Ten of Hearts beats a plain Ace of Acorns in Hearts Solo.
- If neither is a trump, the higher plain_rank of the led suit wins, and an off-suit non-trump loses.
(4) Treat trumps as their own suit for follow-suit checks, so an Ober or Unter in a Solo never counts as its printed suit.
(5) Offer face-up stack cards (stack1_up and stack2_up) as available plays alongside hand cards; the R5 failure shows a face-up card was never offered. Reveal the face-down card only after the trick.
(6) Add both cards' points to the trick winner's hand_points before hand scoring. Then compare the declarer's hand_points with contract_bid, award base × multiplier (+1 for all 8 tricks) to the right player, and add hand_points to card_total.

triage.reason: The full-play tests (R2, R3) start from a real deal and ran without error, so trick play itself works. Only the four scenarios that inject a mid-hand state crashed. Those scenarios use internal names the test writer guessed (round_in_hand, leader, follower, hand, stack1_up, hand_points, a 'led card'), so the game's own bookkeeping, such as its led_card, did not match a card in its card table.
triage.guidance: Do not inject a mid-hand state built from guessed internal variable names. The game's private bookkeeping (who leads, the led card, card-name format, per-hand point counters, which round of the hand it is) is not part of the interface. Either drive scenarios from the real start of the match and assert only the interface attributes (match_points, card_total, bid, hand_number, declarer, contract_bid, contract, multiplier), or set only interface attributes in `given`. Avoid predicting specific card outcomes that depend on the random deal. Check R1, R5 and R12 through offered/not_offered options and through final scores that hold for any deal, or move those card-ranking checks to a deterministic end-of-hand check that does not depend on guessed internal state.

triage.reason: The game was built faithfully, but the design exceeds the platform's budgets: 5 choice steps per round against a limit of 4, and 87 attributes against a limit of 80. It also has a degenerate strategy: always picking the first option wins about 70% of games for either seat, and always picking the last option loses over 80%.
triage.guidance: Simplify the rules so each round needs at most 4 choices and the game fits well under 80 attributes. 1) Cut a choice step from the bidding round. Either drop Stoß entirely (multiplier fixed at 1) or merge the contract choice into the bid, so a single sealed poll picks both, e.g. 'Pass / 53 Solo-of-X / 66 Wenz…', or with fewer contracts. 2) Reduce the state and parameters. Drop the face-down/face-up stacks (deal 8 private cards each from the 16-card deck), or keep one contract type only (e.g. just Wenz, or one fixed trump order), which removes most of the ten trump_strength parameters and the per-stack bookkeeping. 3) Rebalance so no fixed option ordering dominates. The first-listed bid/card should not be a safe default. Make passing carry a cost (e.g. when both pass, the hand is replayed with a penalty, or the passer who becomes declarer has a reduced target), and check that the lowest bid is not almost always made while higher bids are almost always lost. Adjust the bid thresholds (e.g. 53/60/66) or the bases so that each bid level is a real risk-reward choice.
